text: Seven chapters built toward exactly the capstone you just finished. Architecture, navigation, tables and relationships, the dictionary and field types, forms and related lists, import sets, and reporting — each one became a tool the next one used, and the capstone used all seven at once.

A guided click-through teaches you to follow a script. It doesn't teach you what to do when there's no script — which is the actual job. Meridian Freight's instance had no onboarding document, same as a real client site on day one, because that's the skill being tested.

This course is course 2 of 14 in the ServiceNow Administrator path. System Administration, right after this one, assumes you can already navigate, read a dictionary, and recognize a related list without being told twice — because it's about to add users, groups, roles, and ACLs on top of this foundation.

Further ahead, Flow Designer courses will build automations that read and write the exact field types this capstone covered — a flow that checks priority or writes to work_notes only makes sense if you already know what kind of field each one is. Scripting courses will query task and incident by name through the GlideRecord API, assuming you already know those tables exist.

Before starting course 3, be honest: can you find a table list on an unfamiliar instance unaided, can you name a dictionary field's type and what it implies, and can you explain what a related list actually shows someone else. If any of those feel shaky, this capstone is worth revisiting first.
That closes ServiceNow Platform Fundamentals. Up next in the path: ServiceNow System Administration — users, groups, roles, and access control, built directly on everything this course just covered.
